title: Platform integration and hardening: one goal reaches a running deployed environment and back out again
description:
THE EPIC-FINAL ROW for epic-3f9b9556 (Deployment platform). Filed by architect-b63fabf3 on 2026-09-05, at the human's direction, when this epic was split out of epic-8ebe6417 and left with no integration-and-hardening row of its own. Highest order in the epic; `get_context.isEpicFinal` should be true when you hold it.

WHY IT EXISTS. Verification here is CONCENTRATED, not smeared: mid-epic rows prove their own slice and move on, and ONE row at the end gates the whole. The five band parents named in dependsOn (5ef1a0a9 repository, 5d309484 deploy, 9ae492b3 secrets, 8f86e105 migrations, 7683a432 monitoring) are each integration-shaped for their OWN band. Nothing in this epic tests what the bands got wrong ABOUT EACH OTHER - and here the bands are a PIPELINE, so that is nearly all of the risk: the scaffold decides what the image builds, the image decides what variables it needs, the variables decide whether migrations can run, and monitoring probes whatever deploy produced.

WHAT THIS ROW OWNS - the five things no single slice could see:

1. ONE GOAL REACHES A RUNNING ENVIRONMENT. Scaffold a repository from a PRD, deploy it, set its variables, migrate its schema, and prove the deployed thing SERVES - health green, on the landed sha. Every band contributes one link; the chain does not exist to be tested until all five have landed.

2. AND BACK OUT AGAIN. Roll it back and prove the previous sha is serving. A deploy path with no proven exit is a one-way door, and the rollback is the half most likely to have been tested only in isolation.

3. NOTHING LEAKS. This is the epic that starts real processes: containers, a disposable PostgreSQL, a probe schedule, backup jobs. Assert that a FAILED deploy, a FAILED migration and an INTERRUPTED verifier each tear their resources down - not just the happy paths. A test that leaks a container or a port makes every later gate on this board inadmissible, and the failure paths are where leaks actually live.

4. NO SECRET SURFACED ANYWHERE ALONG THE CHAIN. task-d0c63cd8 (DONE) made variables encrypted at rest. This row proves the whole PIPELINE honours it: grep the delivered artifacts - deploy logs, probe output, incident cards, receipts, error paths, generated infrastructure files, and any fixture committed to the tree - for a planted canary value, and assert zero hits. Assert the canary was actually planted and actually reached the deployed process, or the sweep proves nothing.

5. THE DOCS SWEEP for this epic, held back from the individual rows so the same file is not re-edited five times.

MEASURED CONTEXT AT FILING (2026-09-05, HEAD f3b94eaa, branch moe/work-2026-09-04): 23 non-archived rows, of which 22 are LIVE and only ONE is DONE. THIS IS THE LEAST-STARTED THIRD OF THE BOARD. Read that as an instruction: when you claim this row, most of what it certifies will have been built recently and by many hands, so re-measure everything and treat this description as stale. This epic also does NOT own the shared runtime roster any more - the environment kinds (task-d0d1cb5c, task-b3888068, task-a2409cba) publish through the same contracts files and the same four digest mirrors as the operator-gates epic, whose rows are NOT visible in your epicSiblings. Census those mirrors yourself with a full-tree `git grep` of the literal across ALL file types.

NOT IN SCOPE: building any band. Every capability here is shipped by a row named in dependsOn. A gap found here becomes a prerequisite production row measured symbol by symbol - never a narrowed DoD, never a mock-backed journey, never authority reimplemented inside a test.

VERIFICATION COMMAND for moe.complete_task: `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test`. Run every leg named in DoD-6 and quote all their count lines.
definitionOfDone: FULL REGRESSION, green, with numbers, across every package this epic touched - `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test`, `pnpm --filter @moe/control-room test`, `pnpm typecheck`, and root `pnpm test`, plus whatever package the scaffold and infrastructure rows created (resolve those legs BY PACKAGE NAME, never by directory: `pnpm --filter <pkg>` prints "No projects matched the filters" and EXITS 0 for a name that is not a workspace package). Quote every `Test Files N passed` count line; an exit-0 leg with no count line RAN NOTHING. Root `pnpm test` covers NO apps/** file, so the app legs are not optional.

ONE GOAL REACHES A RUNNING DEPLOYED ENVIRONMENT, end to end and for real: a repository scaffolded from a PRD, deployed at a landed sha, its variables delivered to the process, its schema migrated, and its health probe GREEN. Assert the deployed thing actually SERVES - an HTTP response from the running environment, not a receipt saying it should be up. Name the sha and quote the probe result.

AND ROLLS BACK: after the deploy above, roll the environment back and prove the PREVIOUS sha is the one now serving, again by response rather than by receipt. Assert the rollback is reachable from the incident path a real operator would use, not only from a test harness.

NOTHING LEAKS ON A FAILURE PATH. Assert teardown for a FAILED deploy, a FAILED migration and an INTERRUPTED verifier - three arms, each proving the container, the disposable database and the port are gone afterwards. Enumerate the live resources before and after by a real query (`docker ps`, a port probe, a process list), not by trusting a cleanup function returned. The happy-path teardown is already each band's own; this clause is only about the failure paths.

NO SECRET SURFACES ANYWHERE ALONG THE PIPELINE. Plant a canary variable value, prove it REACHED the deployed process (or the sweep is vacuous), then grep every delivered artifact for it - deploy logs, probe output, incident cards, receipts, error paths, generated infrastructure files, and any fixture committed to the tree - and assert zero hits. Quote the canary's shape (not its value) and the exact paths swept.

THE ADVERSARIAL PASS over the WHOLE EPIC DIFF plus THE DOCS SWEEP, in one pass each. The pass looks for what the bands got wrong about each other, not at any band alone: a scaffold that generates infrastructure the deploy path cannot consume; a variable name the app expects and the environment store spells differently; a migration that works alone but not in sequence after a rollback; a probe schedule that outlives the environment it probes; a refusal code whose layer disagrees across two bands. Record what was checked AND what was found - a pass that finds nothing must say what it looked for. The docs sweep covers the operator-facing words for all five bands and any doc that still describes the platform as unbuilt.
taskRails: THIS ROW BUILDS NO BAND. Every capability it certifies is shipped by a row named in dependsOn. A gap found here becomes a prerequisite production row with the gap measured symbol by symbol - never a narrowed DoD, a mock-backed journey, or authority reimplemented inside a test. A proof that only proves shapes retires the question unanswered.

ANYTHING THIS ROW STARTS, IT STOPS - and it proves the FAILURE paths stop too. Enumerate live containers, databases and ports by real query before and after; a cleanup function that returned is not evidence the resource is gone. A leaked container or port makes every later gate on this board inadmissible.

A SECRET NEVER SURFACES IN PLAINTEXT - not on a screen, not in a log line, not in a receipt, not in an error path, not in a generated infrastructure file, not in a fixture committed to the tree. And a canary sweep that cannot prove the canary was planted and delivered proves nothing.

THE SHARED RUNTIME ROSTER IS OWNED BY A DIFFERENT EPIC. The environment kinds publish through the same contracts files and the same four digest mirrors as the operator-gates epic, whose rows will NOT appear in your epicSiblings. Census the mirrors yourself with a full-tree `git grep` across ALL file types, and run `pnpm --filter @moe/control-room test` - two mirrors are invisible to `pnpm test`, `pnpm typecheck` and the daemon leg.

RE-MEASURE BEFORE PLANNING. At filing, 22 of this epic's 23 rows were unstarted - so nearly everything this row certifies will be recently built by many hands. Treat every claim in this description as stale by default and read the dependsOn rows' completionSummary and reviewSummary from epicSiblings first.
FEATURES ONLY (inherited): no security-boundary or policy work.

implementationPlan.description:
MEASURE THE TWO THINGS THAT DECIDE WHETHER THIS ROW CAN COMPLETE, before any code.

A. THE FIVE BANDS. All five dependsOn parents were unlanded at plan time. For each, read `completionSummary` and `reviewSummary` from `get_context.epicSiblings` FIRST (rail 5 directs that instead of re-measuring HEAD), then spot-check on disk what they do not cover:
  `git grep -c "deployment.deploy\|deployment.rollback\|moe-migration-receipt\|moe-health-probe\|environment.set_variable" -- apps packages`
Each returned NOTHING at plan time. A gap found here becomes a PREREQUISITE PRODUCTION ROW measured symbol by symbol (rail 1) - never a narrowed DoD, never a mock, never authority reimplemented in a test.

B. DOCKER. Run `docker version --format "{{.Server.Version}}"` and record the verbatim output. At plan time this host answered:
  failed to connect to the docker API at npipe:////./pipe/dockerDesktopLinuxEngine ... The system cannot find the file specified.
IF DOCKER IS STILL ABSENT, DoD 2, 3 AND 4 CANNOT BE HONESTLY MET: DoD 2 demands an HTTP response from a running environment rather than a receipt, DoD 3 demands the previous sha be SERVING, DoD 4 demands live resources enumerated by real query. Do steps 2, 6 and 7 (which need no docker), then `moe.report_blocked` with this measurable unblock condition:
  "a host with a running docker daemon; verify with `docker version --format {{.Server.Version}}` returning a version"
quoting the failure verbatim and listing exactly which DoD items remain. That is the shape task-3706b7e7 used and the governor endorsed. DO NOT assert a receipt in place of a response, DO NOT mock the container, DO NOT skip the arm - each converts a blocked clause into a false green.

FULL REGRESSION (DoD 1) — runs regardless of docker, so do it before any blocking decision.

Each leg standalone, each quoted with its `Test Files N passed` count line. An exit-0 leg with NO count line RAN NOTHING, and `pnpm --filter <pkg> <script>` prints "No projects matched the filters" and EXITS 0 for a name that is not a workspace package — so resolve every leg BY PACKAGE NAME, never by directory:
- `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test`
- `pnpm --filter @moe/control-room test`
- `pnpm typecheck`
- `pnpm test` (root lane)
- plus whatever package the scaffold and infrastructure rows created. Find its NAME first: `git grep -l '"name"' -- '**/package.json'` and match against what those rows shipped.

State plainly that root `pnpm test` covers NO `apps/**` file, so the two app legs are not optional and a bare root count line is not evidence for them.

EXPECT FOREIGN RED AND ATTRIBUTE IT RATHER THAN CHASING IT: the governor's 19:26Z/19:30Z logs record `mtkbtsvc` handle exhaustion making full-suite runs time out at 30 s in files nobody owns (`src/work/foundation-capture-producer.test.ts` named repeatedly). Apply the path-attributed baseline — merge-base failures, HEAD failures, subtract, intersect with this row's owned paths. Disclose foreign red verbatim with paths; do NOT re-run a full suite repeatedly, which degrades every other seat's gate.

Keep this run: it is the merge-base half of the baseline the completion record needs.

AND BACK OUT AGAIN (DoD 3) — same file, needs docker.

After the deploy in step 3, roll the environment back and prove THE PREVIOUS SHA IS NOW SERVING — again BY RESPONSE, not by receipt. Assert the response identifies the previous build, so "something is up" cannot pass for "the rollback worked".

ASSERT THE ROLLBACK IS REACHABLE FROM THE INCIDENT PATH A REAL OPERATOR WOULD USE, not only from a test harness. DoD 3 names this specifically, and it is the clause that catches a rollback proven only in isolation: the operator's route is the incident card's offered control, which rests on a daemon offer. Drive it that way.

A DEPLOY PATH WITH NO PROVEN EXIT IS A ONE-WAY DOOR. This is the half most likely to have been tested only within its own band, because every band can rehearse its own rollback against its own fixture and none of them exercises the sequence after a real migration.

Assert what happened to the SCHEMA across the rollback: the migration ran before the rollback, so state whether the schema stayed migrated or was reverted, and confirm that matches what the migration and rollback rows actually shipped. A rollback that silently leaves a forward schema under a previous build is a cross-band defect no single band can see — exactly this row's subject.

NOTHING LEAKS ON A FAILURE PATH (DoD 4) — `tests/e2e/foundation/platform-teardown-failure-paths.e2e.test.ts`. Needs docker.

THREE ARMS, all on FAILURE paths, because the happy-path teardown is each band's own and the leaks live here:
1. a FAILED deploy;
2. a FAILED migration;
3. an INTERRUPTED verifier.

For each, ENUMERATE LIVE RESOURCES BEFORE AND AFTER BY REAL QUERY — `docker ps`, a port probe, a process list. DoD 4 forbids trusting a cleanup function that returned, and rail 2 says the same: a returned cleanup is not evidence the resource is gone. Diff the before and after sets and assert the delta is empty.

Assert the container, the disposable database AND the port — all three, per arm. A test that checks containers and leaves a port bound has proven the least interesting third.

INTERRUPT MEANS INTERRUPT: kill the verifier rather than returning an error from it. A function that returns an error unwinds its own `finally`; a killed process does not, and that difference is the whole reason this arm exists.

This test must not itself leak while proving others do not — its own teardown runs in a `finally`, and it records what it started so a failure names the orphan. A leaked container or port makes every later gate on this board inadmissible, and this row's neighbours are already blocked on exactly that class of failure.

NO SECRET SURFACES ANYWHERE (DoD 5) — `tests/e2e/foundation/platform-secret-canary.e2e.test.ts`. The COMMITTED-ARTIFACT half runs WITHOUT docker; do that half even when blocking.

PLANT A CANARY variable value, then PROVE IT WAS PLANTED AND ACTUALLY REACHED THE DEPLOYED PROCESS. DoD 5 and rail 3 both say a sweep that cannot prove delivery proves nothing: a grep finding zero hits is equally consistent with perfect secrecy and with a canary that was never set. Assert delivery first, then sweep. Without docker, prove delivery as far as the pipeline reaches and say exactly where the proof stops.

THEN GREP EVERY DELIVERED ARTIFACT for the canary and assert ZERO hits: deploy logs, probe output, incident cards, receipts, error paths, generated infrastructure files, and any fixture committed to the tree. Quote the exact paths swept — an unenumerated sweep is not reproducible.

QUOTE THE CANARY'S SHAPE, NEVER ITS VALUE (DoD 5). And choose a value that cannot occur naturally but does NOT look like a real credential: a plausible-looking secret in a test trips credential scanners and becomes its own incident.

SWEEP THE ERROR PATHS DELIBERATELY, not just the success ones — that is where a value leaks. A failed health probe echoing a connection string, a migration error quoting a DSN, a docker command logged with `-e` arguments: each is a real shape and each is invisible on a green run.

Also sweep the GENERATED INFRASTRUCTURE FILES from the scaffold and infrastructure rows — a value baked into a generated docker-compose or Dockerfile is committed, not merely logged.

THE ADVERSARIAL PASS OVER THE WHOLE EPIC DIFF (DoD 6, first half) — no docker needed, so do it regardless.

Not a re-review of any band. Look for what the five bands got wrong ABOUT EACH OTHER, because here they are a PIPELINE and that is where nearly all the risk sits. Hunt each of these specifically, with a command:
- A SCAFFOLD THAT GENERATES INFRASTRUCTURE THE DEPLOY PATH CANNOT CONSUME. Diff the generated Dockerfile/compose against what the deploy effect's argv actually expects.
- A VARIABLE NAME THE APP EXPECTS AND THE ENVIRONMENT STORE SPELLS DIFFERENTLY. Compare the scaffold's `.env.example` names against the required-names the contract carries and against what delivery sets. This is a pure cross-band defect and no band's own tests can see it.
- A MIGRATION THAT WORKS ALONE BUT NOT IN SEQUENCE AFTER A ROLLBACK (step 4 exercises it; record the finding here).
- A PROBE SCHEDULE THAT OUTLIVES THE ENVIRONMENT IT PROBES — tear an environment down and confirm the schedule stops rather than probing a dead URL forever.
- A REFUSAL CODE WHOSE LAYER DISAGREES ACROSS TWO BANDS. Grep each band's codes and compare their layer literals; the same code attributed to two layers is a real defect this board has produced before.
- THE DIGEST MIRRORS (rail 4): census BY HEX across ALL file types, never by symbol — three of four mirrors hard-code the hex and one is a `.tsx`. Confirm every mirror carries the CURRENT digest, and run `pnpm --filter @moe/control-room test`, which is the only leg that can see two of them.

RECORD WHAT WAS CHECKED AND WHAT WAS FOUND. A pass that finds nothing MUST say what it looked for — an unqualified "no issues" is not a result. Put the list in a row comment under ~4500 chars. Anything found that is not this row's to fix becomes a prerequisite row or a comment, never a silent fix inside an epic-final row.

FOLD-IN from architect-aa54e231, 2026-09-05. You are this epic's integration-and-hardening row, and two DoD items from task-f008f29a38d54ae7a10e97cad1c4443d belong here rather than in a third UI grandchild. Filed as a comment per global rail 21 and the COMPLETION EVIDENCE rail; nothing below needs a new row.

WHY THIS LANDED ON YOU. task-f008f29a ("The operator sees an environment go down and rolls it back from the incident card") measured at thirteen-plus files against the ten-file ceiling, so I split its four UI surfaces into two grandchildren:
  - task-df972c274f2a43eda3a9f57d2780c6f9 (order 123.1) - the Environments surface: UP/DEGRADED/DOWN, latency sparkline, backups list with restore-proof state.
  - task-85895a88a2484d8589046b2030efd445 (order 123.2) - the Needs-you incident card: verbatim error line, rollback confirm naming the sha, dismiss-is-not-resolve.
Its remaining two items are the PROOF, and `moe.create_task` named you when I filed the first grandchild. Your own title - "one goal reaches a running deployed environment and back out again" - is already the journey those items describe, so folding beats a third row. The epic is at 44 non-archived rows against an advisory ceiling of 40, which makes adding one worse than folding.

ADD TO YOUR DoD (verbatim from task-f008f29a's DoD 6 and 7, with the parts that are now other rows' responsibility stripped):

(1) A PLAYWRIGHT JOURNEY AGAINST A REAL DAEMON covering DOWN -> incident card -> rollback -> recovery, with the `pnpm test:e2e:browser` count line quoted. Note `pnpm test:e2e:browser` runs `tsc -p tests/e2e/control-room/tsconfig.json` FIRST, so a harness type error fails the leg before any test runs and a tsc failure is not a test result.

(2) A LIVE DRIVE: a deployed PREVIEW environment probed for at least 10 minutes, a FORCED failure raising the incident card, and a rollback restoring the previous sha. Record a probe-ring excerpt and the receipts in a row comment under ~4500 chars (comments truncate SILENTLY at 5000). IF NO ENVIRONMENT IS DEPLOYED, RECORD THAT PLAINLY RATHER THAN SIMULATING IT - the deployment row is a sibling that may not have landed, and a simulated live drive is worth less than an honest absence.

(3) The runbook and README updated for the Environments surface and the incident/rollback flow.

TWO THINGS TO CARRY, both measured while planning the parent, so you do not rediscover them:

- THE DAEMON-SIDE INCIDENT AND THE UI CARD ARE DIFFERENT DELIVERABLES, deliberately. Needs-you is a control-room model over a CLOSED roster (needs-you-model.ts:28) whose items are "derived only from things the daemon already states" and which all route to a GOAL. A deployment outage routes to an ENVIRONMENT, so the fifth kind is a UI change: task-cc05c47362dc41b0b2b416a70ad45b42 writes the durable incident record and task-85895a88 renders the card. When you grade "exactly one incident", the durable record is where that property lives; the card is downstream of it.

- THE PROBE SCHEDULE IS THE DAEMON'S FIRST RECURRING LOOP. `grep -rn "setInterval" apps/daemon/src --include=*.ts` excluding tests returned ZERO at plan time, so task-e651725c92434127a7b8d72f0ac5246b builds it. For your whole-epic pass that means one specific thing worth checking: after everything lands, that grep should show ONE scheduler and no second armed timer anywhere in the probe or deploy code. A second independently-armed interval is the double-schedule hazard arriving by a route the scheduler's own tests cannot see, and its only symptom is a durable store filling twice as fast - never an error.

FOLLOW-UP ITEM FOR THIS EPIC-FINAL HARDENING ROW — filed as a comment rather than a new row, by agreement between qa-d81848bc, governor-afbde490 and me (architect-b63fabf3, 2026-09-06 15:4xZ). QA originally said it "deserves its own row" and withdrew that on learning this epic is at 57 non-archived rows against a ceiling of 40. **Small, real, and worth one arm.**

## THE LATENT TRAP: `requiredCapability` has TWO homes and only one is live

Surfaced by worker-96c6d708's mutation drill on task-6d5db404 (the `repository.bootstrap` ADMIN widening, DONE at `2735406c`), then independently re-derived by qa-d81848bc in that row's review.

**MEASURED AT HEAD:**
```
daemon-command-registry.ts:314-320  entryOf: const asyncEntry = asyncEntries[kind];
                                    if (asyncEntry !== undefined) return commandAuthority.wrapAsync(asyncEntry);
                                    // "Answered first and returned whole... none of the
                                    //  synchronous wiring below applies to it."
daemon-command-async-entries.ts:315 requiredCapability: CAPABILITIES.ADMIN,     <- THE SERVED VALUE
daemon-command-vocabulary.ts:69     "repository.bootstrap": CAPABILITIES.ADMIN  <- DEAD for this kind
```

`http-command-ingress.ts:158` reads `entry.requiredCapability`. For an **async-served** kind that entry comes from the async-entries hardcode; `commandFamilyFacts` is never consulted, so `BOOTSTRAP_FAMILY`'s entry is dead weight.

**THE PROOF THAT IT IS A TRAP, not a theory:** mutating `ADMIN -> GOAL` at `vocabulary:69` yields **8/8 GREEN**. Mutating the same value at `async-entries:315` reds **4 arms**, including the paired-human-without-ADMIN refusal. QA ran both.

**WHY IT MATTERS:** anyone tightening or loosening a capability in the vocabulary — the obvious place to look — sees every test stay green and concludes the served behaviour changed. It did not. On `repository.bootstrap` that is a capability guarding repository creation at an operator-supplied filesystem path.

## WHAT THIS ROW SHOULD DO — either shape is fine, both are small

- **(a) Delete the dead entry** for async-served kinds, so there is one home. Cleanest, but check nothing else reads `BOOTSTRAP_FAMILY` for those kinds first.
- **(b) Assert the two agree** — a test that, for every async-served kind, compares the async entry's `requiredCapability` against the family map's entry and fails on drift. Keeps both (some readers may want the map complete) and makes divergence loud.

**(b) is my recommendation** if any consumer legitimately reads the map for async kinds; **(a) if none does.** One grep settles it.

## RAIL THIS IS AN INSTANCE OF

Same family as the derived-roster gotcha: **find what the running code READS, not what the constant is NAMED.** Both lines say `CAPABILITIES.ADMIN` and look interchangeable; only one is served. A grep for the symbol finds both and tells you nothing about which is authoritative.

Not in scope for any in-flight row. No dependency; this row can take it whenever it runs its hardening pass.

planningNotes.approachesConsidered:
PLANNING AROUND THE MISSING DOCKER DAEMON. Rejected, and this is the row's central judgement. The available shortcuts are all forbidden: asserting a receipt instead of an HTTP response narrows DoD 2's explicit wording; mocking the container fabricates the authority the row exists to certify; and skipping the arm silently converts a blocked clause into a green one. DELIVERY BIAS permits a hard block exactly when proceeding would fabricate authority, and this is that case. The plan therefore does every docker-independent clause, and blocks on the rest with a measurable unblock condition - the same shape task-3706b7e7 used and the governor endorsed.

WHAT IS STILL PROVABLE WITHOUT DOCKER, and it is not nothing: the full regression legs (DoD 1), the canary sweep over COMMITTED artifacts and GENERATED INFRASTRUCTURE FILES (part of DoD 5), the cross-band adversarial pass over the whole epic diff (DoD 6), and the docs sweep (DoD 6). Those are planned to run regardless, so a docker host later has only the live clauses left.

SPLITTING THE ROW. Rejected. Its whole value is that ONE row sees what five bands got wrong about each other; splitting it by clause would recreate the smeared verification the epic-final pattern exists to prevent. Six files, eight steps.

WRITING A FIFTH HARNESS for the journey. Rejected - tests/e2e/foundation already has four real-process harnesses; reuse their store-construction and teardown shape.

1. THIS HOST HAS NO DOCKER DAEMON, AND DoD 2, 3 AND 4 CANNOT BE HONESTLY MET WITHOUT ONE. Measured directly:
